title: Agni Loses His Appetite
hookLine: Agni falls sick from too much ghee; the Gita says that same fire lives in every body, so a meal is an offering, fed well in winter
carry: eating is an offering to the fire within
tomorrow: why does spring ask you to go lighter?

cards: Agni, the god of fire, is sick. A king named Shvetaki has spent years pouring ghee into sacrificial fires, and Agni has had to take in all of it. Now he's pale, sluggish, and he's lost his appetite.
Fire, off his food. So he goes to Brahma, the creator, and asks what's wrong with him.

teach.b: This is from the Mahabharata's first book. Brahma's answer is a change of diet: the right fuel will restore you.
Agni's cure comes at a fierce cost, the burning of the Khandava forest, with Krishna and Arjuna helping him, and the epic doesn't hide how terrible that fire is.
But hold on to the picture at the start: fire can be overfed, and fire can be hungry. Here's the teaching. In Hinduism, the fire that digests your food is Agni too.
In the Gita, Krishna says: I become Vaishvanara, the fire in the bodies of living beings, and joined with the breath, I digest the food. So eating is an offering into a sacred fire.

That's why many Hindus say a Gita verse before meals, brahmarpanam: the offering is Brahman, the food is Brahman, poured by Brahman into the fire that is Brahman. Ayurveda builds its seasons around the same fire.
The Charaka Samhita says that in the cold months, hemanta and shishira, the inner fire is held in by the cold and grows strong, and needs warm, substantial food.
Starve it, the text warns, and it turns on the body's own tissues. And at Makar Sankranti in midwinter, families give each other sesame and jaggery: winter food, shared.
Today, a bigger appetite on a cold day isn't a failing to fight; on this teaching it's a fire doing its work.
And any meal can be offered before it's eaten. Many Christians say grace, thanking God for the food; the Hindu verse goes on to call the eating itself worship.

how: Many Hindus say the Gita's brahmarpanam verse before meals, offering the food to God; Ayurveda advises warm, substantial food in the cold months, and in parts of India families share sesame-and-jaggery sweets at Makar Sankranti.

o: a year read season by season; winter feeds a strong fire
one fixed diet, kept the same through the whole year
the festival days that fall in the cold months only

games.q: the fire within — tap the pairs.
p: the Gita verse said before meals
the cold months, a strong fire

s: in the Gita, Krishna says he is the fire that digests food in living bodies
as Vaishvanara, joined with the breath.
Charaka says winter is the season to eat as little as possible
the cold makes the inner fire strong, and it needs substantial food.
Hindu mealtime prayer is only a thank-you
brahmarpanam offers the meal, and the eating, as worship of Brahman.

games.q: deep winter, you're starving by lunch, and someone says a big appetite is weakness. what's the Hindu read?
o: the inner fire is strong in the cold: feed it well, and offer the meal first.
eat cold food to calm the fire down.
games.why: Charaka says the cold holds the fire in and makes it strong; the Gita calls that fire Vaishvanara, so the meal is an offering.

practice: Find the warmest place in the body right now, the chest or the belly, and rest your attention there, feeling the out-breath warm as it leaves. Then picture your next meal.

Many Hindus fold their hands before eating and say brahmarpanam, offering the food first; if you pray, you can try that at your next meal, and if you don't, take one breath of thanks before the first bite.

wordCard.voice: The seasons. In winter, Charaka reads a strong inner fire held in by the cold; the Gita calls that fire Vaishvanara, God in the body.

orig.note: Sanskrit Vaishvanara: 'belonging to all people', a name of Agni; in the Gita, the fire in every body that digests food.

carryVoice: Your line: eating is an offering to the fire within. Agni, fed well. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, the burning of the Khandava forest (Agni sated and sickened by King Shvetaki's long sacrifice; Brahma's counsel; Krishna and Arjuna help him)
Bhagavad Gita 15.14 (as Vaishvanara, in the bodies of living beings, joined with prana and apana, I digest the four kinds of food) and 4.24 (brahmarpanam: the offering is Brahman...)
Charaka Samhita, Sutrasthana 6 (the chapter on the seasons: hemanta and shishira; the strong digestive fire in the cold; the winter regimen)
